newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- Front-end FX vols off highs as dlr pauses.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- Front-end FX vols off highs as dlr pauses.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/yen options, particularly the shorter dates, slipped from overnight highs as the dollar took a pause in the U.S. after an earlier spike above 126.50 yen, dealers said.
The back end also softened somewhat, but to a lesser extent due to resurgent perception that fundamentals overwhelmingly favored the dollar, they added.

"Most people think something extraordinary has to happen to stop the dollar's uptrend," said Masao Okada, chief options trader at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank. "So there's a lot of buying interest at lower levels in both spot and volatilities."
Although the shorter dates were more liable to corrections under the gravity of time-decay, they remained very sensitive to a higher spot, said a trader at a European bank in Chicago.
"They would certainly snap back if the currency goes higher again," he said. "More so in dollar/yen than dollar/mark."

Implied volatility for one-month dollar/yen options was down some 0.4 point from overnight highs and off nearly a quarter point from late Monday to about 10.4/10.6 percent in early afternoon U.S. business.
One-year lost 0.2 from the highs to 10.85/10.95 percent.
Due to some large U.S. fund buying recently in back-end options with strike prices around 130-135 yen, bank dealers were collectively short such options, traders said.

"If both the dollar and volatilities keep rising, there is going to be a lot of bloodshed," Okada at DKB said. Longer-dated options are rich in vega, the rate of change in premiums per move in implied volatility levels.
"If someone comes in looking for low-delta yen calls, I think a lot of dealers would be happy to do a risk reversal, selling those options and buying yen puts," he noted.
"It's better to be short $50 million each in both upside and downside strikes than to be short $100 million in the upside strike," he said.

By buying $50 million worth of low-delta yen puts and selling $50 million of low-delta yen calls in a risk-reversal, a dealer who had been short $100 million of the upside strike will have evened out his risk exposure without significantly changing his volatility position at present spot levels.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal stood at 0.3/0.5 point in favor of yen puts, unchanged from Monday. It was at around par as recently as last Thursday.
Dollar/mark volatilities were weaker as the dollar hovered below resistance near 1.72 marks.

Although the greenback's strength against the yen supported dollar/mark, views on its long-term trend appeared less one-sided than in dollar/yen because of uncertainty surrounding a single European currency, traders said.
One-month and one-year dollar/mark implied volatilities stood at 9.3/9.5 and 9.4/9.6 percent respectively, compared with just below 10 percent in both maturities on Monday.
One-month 25-delta risk reversal was 0.1/0.3 point skewed for mark puts.
